section.heading: 8.4. The Method of Least Squares
The Method of Least Squares
section.paragraph: In Section 1.4, Example 10, we saw how a linear equation can be used to approximate the sales trend for a local sporting goods store. As we saw there, one use of a trend line is to predict a store’s future sales. Recall that we obtained the line by requiring that it pass through two data points, the rationale being that such a line seems to fit the data reasonably well.

In this section, we describe a general method, known as the method of least squares , for determining a straight line that, in some sense, best fits a set of data points when the points are scattered about a straight line. To illustrate the principle behind the method of least squares, suppose, for simplicity, that we are given five data points,
that describe the relationship between the two variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ . By plotting these data points, we obtain a graph called a scatter diagram (Figure 22).

image.alt: Details Five points are plotted on the x y coordinate plane: P_1 at (2, 2), P_2 at (3, 6). P_3 at (5, 8), P_4 at (6, 5), and P_5 at (8, 10).

section.paragraph: If we try to fit a straight line to these data points, the line will miss the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth data points by the amounts $$d_{1}$$ , $$d_{2}$$ , $$d_{3}$$ , $$d_{4}$$ , and $$d_{5}$$ , respectively (Figure 23).

image.alt: Details A line and 5 points are plotted in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. Both the horizontal axis x and the vertical axis y ranges from 0 to 10. The line enters the first quadrant through the vertical axis around (0, 1.5), slopes upward slanting to the right and exits the viewing window at the top right around the coordinate (9.5, 10.5). The first point is plotted below the line, around (2, 2) which deviates from the line at a distance of d_1. The second point is plotted above the line, around (3, 6) which deviates from the line at a distance of d_2. The third point is plotted above the line, around (5, 8) which deviates from the line at a distance of d_3. The fourth point is plotted below the line around (6, 5) which deviates from the line at a distance of d_4. The fifth point is plotted above the line around (8.1, 10) which deviates from the line at a distance of d_5.

figure.caption: The approximating line misses the points by the amounts $$d_{1},d_{2},\ldots,d_{5}$$ , respectively.

section.paragraph: The principle of least squares states that the straight line $$L$$ that fits the data points best is the one chosen by requiring that the sum of the squares of $$d_{1}$$ , $$d_{2}$$ , $$d_{3}$$ , $$d_{4}$$ , $$d_{5}$$ —that is,

be made as small as possible. If we think of the amount $$d_{1}$$ as the error made when the value $$y_{1}$$ is approximated by the corresponding value of $$y$$ lying on the straight line $$L$$ , $$d_{2}$$ as the error made when the value $$y_{2}$$ is approximated by the corresponding value of $$y$$ , and so on, then it can be seen that the least-squares criterion calls for minimizing the sum of the squares of the errors. The line $$L$$ obtained in this manner is called the least-squares line , or regression line .
To find a method for computing the regression line $$L$$ , suppose $$L$$ has representation $$y = f(x) = mx + b$$ , where $$m$$ and $$b$$ are to be determined. Observe that

$$\begin{array}{l} {{d_{1}^{2} + d_{2}^{2} + d_{3}^{2} + d_{4}^{2} + d_{5}^{2}} = \left\lbrack {f\left( x_{1} \right) - y_{1}} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {f\left( x_{2} \right) - y_{2}} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {f\left( x_{3} \right) - y_{3}} \right\rbrack^{2}{+ \left\lbrack {f\left( x_{4} \right) - y_{4}} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {f\left( x_{5} \right) - y_{5}} \right\rbrack^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{d_{1}^{2} + d_{2}^{2} + d_{3}^{2} + d_{4}^{2} + d_{5}^{2}} = \left( {mx_{1} + b - y_{1}} \right)^{2} + \left( {mx_{2} + b - y_{2}} \right)^{2} + \left( {mx_{3} + b - y_{3}} \right)^{2}{+ \left( {mx_{4} + b - y_{4}} \right)^{2} + \left( {mx_{5} + b - y_{5}} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$
and may be viewed as a function of the two variables $$m$$ and $$b$$ . Thus, the least-squares criterion is equivalent to minimizing the function

$$\begin{array}{lcl} {f(m,b)} & = & {\left( {mx_{1} + b - y_{1}} \right)^{2} + \left( {mx_{2} + b - y_{2}} \right)^{2} + \left( {mx_{3} + b - y_{3}} \right)^{2}} \\ & & {+ \left( {mx_{4} + b - y_{4}} \right)^{2} + \left( {mx_{5} + b - y_{5}} \right)^{2}} \end{array}$$
with respect to $$m$$ and $$b$$ . To find the minimum of $$f\left( {m,b} \right)$$ , we use the Chain Rule and compute

$$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial b} & = & {2\left( {mx_{1} + b - y_{1}} \right) + 2\left( {mx_{2} + b - y_{2}} \right) + 2\left( {mx_{3} + b - y_{3}} \right)} \\ & & {+ 2\left( {mx_{4} + b - y_{4}} \right) + 2\left( {mx_{5} + b - y_{5}} \right)} \\ & = & {2\left\lbrack {\left( {x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} + x_{4} + x_{5}} \right)m + 5b - \left( {y_{1} + y_{2} + y_{3} + y_{4} + y_{5}} \right)} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$

note.title: Applied Example 2. A Firm’s Advertising Expense and Profit
note.heading: Applied Example 2. A Firm’s Advertising Expense and Profit
note.paragraph: The proprietor of Leisure Travel Service compiled the following data relating the firm’s annual profit to its annual advertising expenditure (both measured in thousands of dollars).

list.item: Determine an equation of the least-squares line for these data.
Draw a scatter diagram and the least-squares line for these data.
Use the result obtained in part (a) to predict Leisure Travel’s annual profit if the annual advertising budget is $$\$ 20,000$$ .

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The calculations required for obtaining the normal equations may be summarized as follows: $$x$$ $$y$$ $$x^{2}$$ $$\mathit{xy}$$ 12 60 144 720 14 70 196 980 17 90 289 1,530 21 100 441 2,100 26 100 676 2,600 30 120 900 3,600 Sum 120 540 2,646 11,530 The normal equations are (13) $$6b + 120m = 540$$ (14) $$120b + 2646m = 11,530$$ Solving Equation (13) for $$b$$ gives (15) $$b = - 20m + 90$$ which, upon substitution into Equation (14), gives $$\begin{array}{rcc} {120\left( {- 20m + 90} \right) + 2646m} & = & {11,530} \\ {- 2400m + 10,800 + 2646m} & = & {11,530} \\ {246m} & = & 730 \\ m & \approx & 2.97 \end{array}$$ Substituting this value of $$m$$ into Equation (15) gives $$b \approx - 20(2.97) + 90 = 30.6$$ Therefore, the required equation of the least-squares line is given by $$y = f(x) \approx 2.97x + 30.6$$

The scatter diagram and the least-squares line are shown in Figure 25. Figure 25 Details A line and 6 points are plotted in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis x, ranges from 0 to 30 and the vertical axis y ranges from 0 to 130. The line enters the first quadrant through the vertical axis around (0, 31), slopes upward slanting to the right and exits the viewing window at the top right around the coordinate (30, 120). The first point is plotted below the line, around (12, 60). The second point is plotted below the line, around (14, 70). The third point is plotted above the line, around (17, 90). The fourth point is plotted above the line around (21, 100). The fifth point is plotted below the line around (26, 100). The sixth point is plotted on the line around (30, 120). The scatter diagram and the least-squares line $$y = 2.97x + 30.6$$

Leisure Travel’s predicted annual profit corresponding to an annual budget of $$\$ 20,000$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{f(20)}{\approx 2.97(20) + 30.6}} \\ {\phantom{f(20)}{= 90}} \end{array}$$ or $$\$ 90,000$$ .

note.title: Applied Example 3. Maximizing Profit
note.heading: Applied Example 3. Maximizing Profit
note.paragraph: A market research study conducted for Century Communications provided the following data based on the projected monthly sales $$x$$ (in thousands) of Century’s DVD version of a box-office hit adventure movie with a proposed wholesale unit price of $$p$$ dollars.

list.item: Find the demand equation if the demand curve is the least-squares line for these data.

The total monthly cost function associated with producing and distributing the DVD movies is given by $$C(x) = 4x + 25$$ where $$x$$ denotes the number of discs (in thousands) produced and sold and $$C(x)$$ is in thousands of dollars. Determine the unit wholesale price that will maximize Century’s monthly profit.

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The calculations required for obtaining the normal equations may be summarized as follows: $$x$$ $$p$$ $$x^{2}$$ $$\mathit{xp}$$ 2.2 38 4.84 83.6 5.4 36 29.16 194.4 7.0 34.5 49 241.5 11.5 30 132.25 345 14.6 28.5 213.16 416.1 Sum 40.7 167 428.41 1280.6 The normal equations are $$\begin{array}{rcc} {5b + 40.7m} & = & 167 \\ {40.7b + 428.41m} & = & 1280.6 \end{array}$$ Solving this system of linear equations simultaneously, we find that $$m \approx - 0.81$$ and $$b \approx 40.00$$ Therefore, the required equation of the least-squares line is given by $$p = f(x) \approx - 0.81x + 40.00$$ which is the required demand equation, provided $$0 \leq x \leq 49.38$$ .

The approximate total revenue function in this case is given by $$R(x) = xp = - 0.81x^{2} + 40.00x$$ Since the total cost function is $$C(x) = 4x + 25$$ we see that the approximate profit function is $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(x)} = {- 0.81x^{2} + 40.00x - \left( {4x + 25} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P(x)} = {- 0.81x^{2} + 36.00x - 25}} \end{array}$$ To find the absolute maximum of $$P(x)$$ over the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,49.38} \right\rbrack$$ , we compute $$P^{\prime}(x) = - 1.62x + 36.00$$ Setting $$P^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ gives $$x \approx 22.22$$ as the only critical point of $$P$$ . Finally, from the table $$\mathbf{x}$$ 0 22.22 49.38 $$\mathbf{P}\left( \mathbf{x} \right)$$ -25 375.00 -222.41 we see that the optimal wholesale price is $$p = - 0.81(22.22) + 40.00 = 22.00$$ or $$\$ 22$$ per disc.

note.source_type: Applied Example 2. Erosion of the Middle Class
note.title: Applied Example 2. Erosion of the Middle Class
note.heading: Applied Example 2. Erosion of the Middle Class
note.paragraph: The idea of a large, stable, middle class (defined as those with annual household incomes in 2010 between $$\$ 39,000$$ and $$\$ 118,000$$ for a family of three), is central to America’s sense of itself. The following table gives the percentage of middle-income adults $$(y)$$ in the United States from 1971 through 2011.
Let $$t$$ be measured in decades with $$t = 0$$ corresponding to 1971.

list.item: Find an equation of the least-squares line for these data.
If this trend continues, what will the percentage of middle-income adults be in 2021?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: First we enter the data as follows: $$\begin{array}{lllll} { x_{1} = 0} & { {y_{1} = 61}} & { {x_{2} = 1}} & { {y_{2} = 59}} & { {x_{3} = 2}} \\ { {y_{3} = 56}} & { {x_{4} = 3}} & { {y_{4} = 54}} & { {x_{5} = 4}} & { {y_{5} = 51}} \end{array}$$ Then, using the linear regression function from the statistics menu, we obtain the output shown in Figure T2. Therefore, an equation of this least-squares line is $$y = - 2.5t + 61.2$$ Figure T2 The TI-83/84 linear regression screen
The percentage of middle-income adults in 2021 will be $$y = - (2.5)(5) + 61.2 = 48.7$$ or approximately $$48.7\%$$ .
